# Beeswarm plots {#sec-beeswa} ::: {.callout-tip appearance='simple' icon=false} ***This graph is largely complete and just needs final proof reading.*** ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false} ::: {style="font-size: 1.25em; color: #02577A;"} :::
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a categorical variable** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** ::: :::: ## Description The beeswarm plot uses points to display the distribution of a continuous variable across the levels of a categorical variable. The points are grouped by level, and the shape (or swarm) of the distribution is mirrored above and below the quantitative axis (similar to a violin plot). We can create beeswarm plot using `geom_jitter()` or the [`ggbeeswarm` package](https://github.com/eclarke/ggbeeswarm). ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} # pak::pak("eclarke/ggbeeswarm") library(ggbeeswarm) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: Tetris came bundled with every Game Boy, and by the 90s everyone had a high score to brag about. We'll simulate the number of lines cleared in 80 games by each of three players. `rnbinom()` draws each game's count from a negative binomial distribution, with a different average (`mu`) for each player: 25 lines for a casual player, 60 for a regular, and 120 for an expert. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 240 games every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1989) tetris_games <- tibble( game_id = 1:240, player = rep(c("Casual", "Regular", "Expert"), each = 80)) |> mutate(player = factor(player, levels = c("Casual", "Regular", "Expert")), lines_cleared = rnbinom(n(), size = 5, mu = c(Casual = 25, Regular = 60, Expert = 120)[as.character(player)])) glimpse(tetris_games) #> Rows: 240 #> Columns: 3 #> $ game_id 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9,… #> $ player Casual, Casual, Casual, Ca… #> $ lines_cleared 42, 6, 21, 30, 15, 36, 31,… ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution A beeswarm plot draws every game as its own point, so it shows the spread of each group directly. Tetris scores are counts, but they're much more spread out than the counts in the dot plot chapters: one bad drop can end a game early, and one good streak can keep it going for a long time. Below we'll move from the games, to a picture, to the formula. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first ten games (all from the casual player). ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(tetris_games$lines_cleared, 10) #> [1] 42 6 21 30 15 36 31 9 26 30 ``` ::: ::: The casual player averages about 25 lines, but these games range from 6 to 42. The summary below shows the variance for each player. For Poisson counts (like the Goosebumps books), the variance would be close to the mean. Here the variance is several times larger than the mean, and the gap grows with the player's skill. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} tetris_games |> group_by(player) |> summarise(mean = mean(lines_cleared), variance = var(lines_cleared), min = min(lines_cleared), max = max(lines_cleared)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: The beeswarms below compare our regular player's 80 games to 80 games drawn from a Poisson distribution with the same average (60 lines). The Poisson swarm is a tight cluster around 60. The negative binomial swarm stretches from single digits to more than twice the average, with a long tail of great games at the top. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} regular_games <- tibble( model = rep(c("Negative binomial", "Poisson"), each = 80), lines_cleared = c( tetris_games$lines_cleared[tetris_games$player == "Regular"], rpois(80, lambda = 60))) ggplot(regular_games, aes(x = model, y = lines_cleared, color = model)) + ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(size = 1.6, show.legend = FALSE) + geom_hline(yintercept = 60, linetype = "dashed", color = "#F5F5F5") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Lines cleared") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/draw_beeswarm-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: The [negative binomial distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution) is a common model for counts that are more spread out than a Poisson distribution allows (called *overdispersion*). With an average $\mu$ and a size (or dispersion) parameter $r$, its variance is: $$ X \sim \text{NB}(\mu, \; r = 5), \quad \text{Var}(X) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{r} $$ The first term ($\mu$) is the Poisson variance, and the second term ($\mu^2 / r$) is the extra spread. For the regular player that's $60 + 3600 / 5 = 780$, compared to just 60 for a Poisson distribution. Because the extra spread grows with $\mu^2$, the expert's games ($\mu = 120$) spread out much more than the casual player's ($\mu = 25$). As $r$ gets larger, the extra term shrinks and the negative binomial turns into a Poisson. Try `size = 500` in `rnbinom()` and the three swarms tighten up. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Create labels with `labs()` - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data` - Map `player` to the `x` axis and `color` - Map `lines_cleared` to the `y` axis - Add the `ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm()` layer (with `alpha`) - Remove the legend with `show.legend = FALSE` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_beeswarm <- labs( title = "Tetris", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Lines cleared in 80 games by each player", x = "Player", y = "Lines cleared") ggp2_beeswarm <- ggplot(data = tetris_games, aes(x = player, y = lines_cleared, color = player)) + ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm(alpha = 2 / 3, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_beeswarm + labs_beeswarm ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: Adjust the size/shape of the swarm using `method =` or the `geom_quasirandom()` function ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_beeswarm-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: ## More info Below is some additional arguments and methods for beeswarm plots. ### `method`
Use method to adjust the shape of the beeswarm (`swarm`, `compactswarm`, `hex`, `square`, `center`, or `centre`) :::: {.column-margin} ::: {style="font-size: 0.95rem;"} Set the point `shape` to `21` to control the `fill` and `color` ::: :::: ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggp2_compact_swarm <- ggplot(data = tetris_games, mapping = aes(x = player, y = lines_cleared, color = player)) + ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm( aes(fill = player), method = 'compactswarm', dodge.width = 0.5, shape = 21, color = "#ffffff", alpha = 2/3, size = 1.7, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_compact_swarm + # add labels labs_beeswarm ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_beeswarm_method-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: ### `side`
For a beeswarm that falls across the vertical axis, use the `side` argument. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggp2_rside_swarm <- ggplot(data = tetris_games, mapping = aes(x = player, y = lines_cleared, color = player)) + ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm( aes(fill = player), side = 1, # right/upwards shape = 21, color = "#ffffff", alpha = 2/3, size = 1.7, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_rside_swarm + # add labels labs_beeswarm ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_beeswarm_side-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: ### `cex`
The `cex` argument controls the "*scaling for adjusting point spacing*" ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggp2_beeswarm_cex <- ggplot(data = tetris_games, mapping = aes(x = player, y = lines_cleared, color = player)) + ggbeeswarm::geom_beeswarm( aes(fill = player), cex = 1.6, shape = 21, color = "#ffffff", alpha = 2/3, size = 1.7, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_beeswarm_cex + # add labels labs_beeswarm ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_beeswarm_cex-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: ### `geom_jitter()`
We can also create a beeswarm using the `geom_jitter()` and setting the `height` and `width`. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggp2_jitter_swarm <- ggplot(data = tetris_games, mapping = aes(x = player, y = lines_cleared, color = player)) + geom_jitter( aes(fill = player), height = 0.05, width = 0.11, shape = 21, color = "#ffffff", alpha = 2 / 3, size = 1.7, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_jitter_swarm + # add labels labs_beeswarm ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](beeswarm_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_beeswarm_jitter-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: :::
